title: Supervision 4 essay
description: Explain how the structural and electrical properties of cardiac muscle enable coordinated, rhythmic pumping of blood while allowing relaxation between beats.
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 4. Write it here in one sitting, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Time. There’s no time limit, but give yourself about 40 minutes. The clock at the top counts the time you spend writing and tells you when you reach 40 minutes. Spend the first few minutes planning, on paper if you like.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your essay, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your essay.
  • Saving. Your essay is saved in this browser as you type, so you won’t lose it if you’re interrupted.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your essay and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Cardiac muscle and the heartbeat
questions.text:
Explain how the structural and electrical properties of cardiac muscle enable coordinated, rhythmic pumping of blood while allowing relaxation between beats.

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Use specific examples and numbers from the lectures, and explain how each one helps to answer the question.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and before the supervision, use it to look back over what you wrote. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers, and the questions it should ask.

What the title asks. “Explain how” asks for mechanisms, and the title names three things to explain: pumping that is coordinated, pumping that is rhythmic, and relaxation between beats. A strong essay is organised around those three demands, and links each of them to the structural and electrical properties that meet it. An essay that describes the action potential and excitation–contraction coupling in detail, but never says what each property does for the heart as a pump, misses the point of the title.

  • Coordination: the cells. Cardiac muscle cells are short and branched, usually with one central nucleus, and they’re joined end to end at intercalated discs. Desmosomes and other anchoring junctions hold the cells together and pass on their force. Gap junctions let current flow from cell to cell, so an action potential spreads through all of them, and the atria, and the ventricles, each work as a functional syncytium. Every cell contracts in every beat, unlike skeletal muscle, whose fibres are electrically separate and are recruited in motor units.
  • Coordination: the conduction system. The fibrous skeleton supports the valves and insulates the atria from the ventricles, so the AV node and the bundle of His are normally the only electrical connection between them. Excitation spreads from the sinoatrial node through the atria. The AV node conducts slowly, and its delay makes up most of the PR interval (normally 0.12 to 0.20 s), so the atria can contract and finish filling the ventricles first. Then the bundle branches and Purkinje fibres conduct fast, down the septum to the apex and up the walls, so the ventricles are excited within about a tenth of a second (the QRS) and contract from the apex towards the outflow tracts.
  • Rhythm: the pacemaker. The cells of the sinoatrial node have no stable resting potential. During diastole they depolarise on their own (the pacemaker potential). Several currents bring them to threshold. The funny current, If, flows through channels that open on hyperpolarisation. It carries both Na+ and K+, but at the potentials of diastole the net current is inward. At the same time an outward K+ current declines, and Ca2+ currents add to the depolarisation. The upstroke of their action potential is carried by Ca2+ through L-type channels, and K+ efflux repolarises them. The SA node sets the rate because it reaches threshold first. The AV node and the Purkinje fibres can pace the heart more slowly if it fails.
  • Rhythm: changing the rate. Sympathetic nerves (noradrenaline on β1-adrenoceptors) steepen the pacemaker potential, so threshold is reached sooner. Parasympathetic nerves in the vagus (acetylcholine on M2 receptors) slow the pacemaker depolarisation and increase the K+ conductance, which makes the maximum diastolic potential more negative. Each depolarisation starts further from threshold and climbs more slowly, so threshold is reached later. The nerves change a rhythm the heart makes for itself, which is why a transplanted heart, whose nerves have been cut, still beats. At rest it beats faster than normal, at about 100 a minute, because it has lost the slowing effect of the vagus.
  • Pumping: the action potential and excitation–contraction coupling. A ventricular cell rests at about −85 to −90 mV. Fast Na+ channels give a rapid upstroke, followed by a brief early repolarisation, and then the plateau, in which Ca2+ coming in through L-type channels roughly balances K+ going out. The action potential spreads into the cell along the T-tubules, where the L-type channels lie close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The Ca2+ that comes in through them triggers the release of much more from it, through ryanodine receptors (RyR2): calcium-induced calcium release. Ca2+ binds troponin C, tropomyosin moves, and cross-bridges cycle. Unlike in skeletal muscle, the trigger depends on Ca2+ entering from outside the cell.
  • Pumping: grading the force. With no motor units to recruit, the force of a beat is graded by the amount of Ca2+ released (which sympathetic stimulation increases) and by length. Cardiac muscle works on the ascending limb of its length–tension relationship, and stretch makes its myofilaments more sensitive to Ca2+ (length-dependent activation, in which titin and the spacing of the filaments play a part). So greater filling gives a stronger contraction, the basis of the Frank–Starling mechanism.
  • Relaxation between beats. The long plateau keeps the Na+ channels inactivated, so the refractory period lasts almost as long as the contraction. Summation and tetanus are impossible, and the heart must at least begin to relax before it can be excited again. Relaxation needs energy. SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum using ATP, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger removes Ca2+ from the cell using the Na+ gradient that the Na+/K+-ATPase maintains, and each cross-bridge needs a fresh ATP to let go of actin. The cells are packed with mitochondria, which make this ATP aerobically, beat after beat. As Ca2+ falls, it leaves troponin, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin again, and the ventricle relaxes and fills.
  • The cycle, and one-way flow. The valves open and close passively, with the pressures on either side of them. Atrial systole tops up the filling of the ventricles. In isovolumetric contraction all the valves are closed (S1 as the AV valves shut). Then comes ejection, and isovolumetric relaxation (S2 as the semilunar valves shut), and filling again. The papillary muscles and chordae tendineae stop the AV valves turning inside out; they don’t open them. A diagram of the cardiac cycle, or a pressure–volume loop, can show all this compactly.
  • Evaluation. Compare cardiac with skeletal muscle where the comparison explains something (a functional syncytium rather than motor units, twitches that can’t sum rather than ones that can fuse into a tetanus, and a trigger that needs extracellular Ca2+ rather than one that doesn’t). Failures show what each property does: heart block when the AV node fails, arrhythmias when conduction or refractoriness go wrong, and a heart that can’t fill properly when relaxation is impaired.

Against the core criteria. Does each paragraph explain how a property meets one of the three demands? Do you take a position early on? You might argue, for example, that the long action potential ties contraction and relaxation together, because its plateau carries in the Ca2+ that triggers each contraction, and its long refractory period means that the heart can’t be excited again until it has begun to relax. Do you use specific numbers and examples, rather than general statements? Does the conclusion draw the threads together?
